questions.question: Using the intersection formula, how many intersection points do 4 lines (no two parallel, no three concurrent) create at most?
Using the same formula, how many intersection points do 5 such lines create at most?
What is the formula for the maximum number of regions created by n lines in a plane (general position)?
questions.rationale: Each new line, in general position, adds as many new regions as the number of existing lines it crosses plus one, leading to the closed form 1 + n + C(n,2).

questions.question: Why does figure counting get significantly more difficult as more lines/shapes are added?
options: It doesn't get more difficult, it stays constant
The number of possible combinations of basic elements grows combinatorially, making visual/manual counting increasingly error-prone
More lines always means fewer figures
Additional lines never create new figures
questions.rationale: As more lines or shapes are added, the number of possible combinations grows combinatorially (not linearly), which is exactly why a systematic method becomes essential.

questions.question: What does the 'layer method' involve?
options: Ignoring all but the outermost layer of a figure
Breaking a complex figure into successive layers or levels and counting figures within and across each layer systematically
Drawing the figure in a different color for each layer
Only applies to circular figures
questions.rationale: The layer method decomposes a complex figure into successive layers, counting figures within each layer and across layer boundaries systematically.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'sweep method' in figure counting?
options: To erase parts of the figure
Systematically scanning across the figure (e.g., left to right) to catch every valid figure boundary in order, avoiding missed cases
To randomly sample sections of the figure
To count only the figure's area, not its boundary
questions.rationale: A sweep method scans systematically across the figure in a fixed order, which helps ensure every valid figure boundary is encountered and none are missed.

questions.question: What does the 'marking method' help prevent?
options: Drawing new lines by mistake
Re-counting the same figure twice, by marking/tracking figures already counted
Missing the outer boundary of the figure
Confusing squares with rectangles
questions.rationale: By marking figures as they're counted, this method prevents the same valid figure from being accidentally counted again later in the process.

questions.question: What is a 'hidden boundary trap'?
options: A boundary that is drawn twice
Mistakenly counting a figure whose boundary is only partially drawn, assuming a missing line segment is actually present
A boundary hidden behind another figure physically
A boundary that changes shape over time
questions.rationale: This trap occurs when a figure looks complete at a glance but is actually missing part of its boundary — assuming it's complete without verifying leads to an incorrect count.

questions.question: What does the 'shared line principle' state?
options: Shared lines make both figures invalid
Multiple figures can validly share the same line segment as part of their boundary, so a shared line shouldn't cause a figure to be miscounted or skipped
Only one figure may ever use a given line segment
Shared lines should always be counted as separate figures
questions.rationale: The shared line principle clarifies that two or more distinct valid figures can legitimately share a common boundary segment — this shouldn't cause confusion or a miscount.

questions.question: What is the 'double counting trap'?
options: Forgetting to count a figure at all
Accidentally counting the same valid figure more than once, usually because it was recognized from two different starting points or directions
Counting a figure that doesn't actually exist
Only counting figures of one specific size
questions.rationale: This trap happens when the same figure is recognized and counted more than once, often because it was approached from two different starting points during the counting process.
